chunks.title: What Bespoke is
chunks.text: Bespoke helps you get a garment made the way you imagine it. You describe what you want in English or Hinglish, pin pictures on a moodboard, and Bespoke turns both into a clear specification that a tailor can cut from. It lists the garment, the neckline, the sleeves, the fit, the length, the fabric, the colour and the details you asked for, part by part. When the design is complete you get a tailor sheet that you can print or save as a PDF, and you can send the design to a maker. Bespoke is a design and specification tool: its job is to make sure the tailor understands you without a long back-and-forth.

chunks.title: How Bespoke works in short
chunks.text: You type or speak a request such as "kurti chahiye, waist pe fitted, neeche se thoda loose, V neck thoda deep, no embroidery". Bespoke reads it and fills an order card, one row for each part of the garment. Where something important is missing, such as sleeve length, fabric or colour, it asks you a few short questions with options to choose from. You can tap any row on the order card to change it, and you can step back if you change your mind. Pictures on the moodboard add suggestions, but your own words always come first. At the end you have a specification and a tailor sheet.

chunks.title: Who Bespoke is for
chunks.text: Bespoke has two kinds of users. Customers describe a garment, build a moodboard and get a tailor-ready specification. Makers, meaning designers and tailors, have their own account where they receive design requests from customers, read the specification, flag missing details and chat with the customer. You can use Bespoke to prepare a design even if you have not chosen a tailor yet, because the tailor sheet is something you can print and take anywhere.

chunks.title: Languages Bespoke understands
chunks.text: You can write in English, in Hinglish (Hindi written in English letters) or in Hindi in Devanagari script, and you can mix them in one sentence. Words such as kurti, lehenga, dheela, gehra, baazu and kamar are understood without translation. Small spelling mistakes are usually forgiven, so "anarkalli" or "georget" still work. The tailor sheet can be shown wholly in English or wholly in Hindi, including the names of the parts, the values and the labels, so you can hand it to a tailor in the language they prefer.

chunks.title: Where the assistant fits in
chunks.text: This help assistant answers questions about using Bespoke: how to describe a garment, how the moodboard works, how to take measurements, what the tailor sheet contains and how to work with a maker. It answers only from Bespoke's own help notes. If the notes do not contain the answer, it says so instead of guessing. It does not design the garment for you, so use the main conversation for that.

chunks.title: Describing a garment: start with the garment
chunks.text: Begin with what the garment is, then add parts and details. "Kurti chahiye" or "I want a maxi dress" is a perfectly good start. Bespoke knows 47 garment types, from kurtis, anarkalis, lehengas and sherwanis to hoodies, blazers, jeans and jumpsuits. If you want a top and a bottom together, say so: "a sweatshirt and pants" becomes a co-ord set with two pieces. You do not need technical words. Bespoke will ask about anything important that you leave out, and you can always change a row on the order card later.

chunks.title: English examples that work well
chunks.text: Here are requests that Bespoke reads well. "A navy blue hoodie, oversized, with thumb holes." "Knee length A-line dress in black georgette, square neck, three-quarter sleeves." "Wedding guest lehenga in maroon with zari work, no sequins." Notice that each one names the garment, then a few parts, then fabric, colour or details. Short sentences and commas both work. You can send your request in one message or in several; each new message adds to the design or changes what you said before.

chunks.title: Hinglish examples that work well
chunks.text: You can write the way you talk. "Kurti chahiye, waist pe fitted, neeche se thoda loose, V neck thoda deep, no embroidery." "Lehenga chahiye shaadi ke liye, maroon, gota patti." "Blouse ka gala gol, baazu chhote, kapda cotton." Words such as thoda (a little), bahut (very), nahi and mat (not), neeche (below) and upar (above) are understood and change how the next word is read. Hinglish and English can be mixed freely in the same sentence.

chunks.title: Saying what you do not want
chunks.text: Say what to leave out as plainly as what to include. "No embroidery", "not too flashy", "lehenga nahi" and "sequins mat dalna" all work. Bespoke removes the value from the design and will not bring it back unless you ask for it again. This is useful for details a tailor might add by habit, such as heavy work on the border. A negative note on a moodboard picture, such as "not this colour", works the same way for that picture.

chunks.title: Softening and strengthening words
chunks.text: Small words change how strongly something is meant. "Thoda" and "slightly" soften a value: "V neck thoda deep" sits between a moderate and a deep neckline. "Bahut", "very" and "ekdum" strengthen it. Bespoke attaches these words to the nearest value in the same clause, so keep the soft or strong word right beside what it describes. "Neeche se loose" applies the loose fit to the lower part only, while "waist pe fitted" applies the fitted fit at the waist.

chunks.title: Describing different parts of one garment
chunks.text: One garment can have different fits and details in different places. Use part words to point at them: neckline or gala, sleeve or baazu, waist or kamar, hip, back or peeche, hem or daman, and lower or neeche. "Fitted at the waist, flared below" gives the upper body one fit and the skirt part another. If you describe the front and the back separately, such as a deeper back neck, Bespoke records them as separate rows.

chunks.title: Details Bespoke has no word for
chunks.text: Sometimes you want something the list of values does not cover: pockets, a drawstring, lining, a particular print. Bespoke keeps these as notes in plain English on the order card and the tailor sheet, so the tailor still sees them. A note is shown as your own words rather than as a chosen value. If you would like a note to be precise, add a measurement or a picture on the moodboard.

chunks.title: Changing your mind
chunks.text: Every step can be taken back, so you can undo any change. Before each message, answer, edit or moodboard reading, Bespoke saves the design and the conversation, and a Back button under the latest reply restores the previous state, up to thirty steps. You can also tap any row on the order card to pick a different value. When your own edit conflicts with something a picture suggested, your edit wins.

chunks.title: What Bespoke asks you
chunks.text: When something important is missing, Bespoke asks a short question and offers options. It asks first about the details that are expensive to get wrong. Neckline depth is asked early because a neckline cut too deep cannot be raised again, and sleeve length and garment length matter for the same reason, since fabric that is cut short cannot be lengthened. Colour and fabric are asked too. Which questions appear depends on the garment: a sweatshirt is asked about hood, crew or turtle necks and about oversized fit, while a kurti is asked about round, V, boat, square or mandarin necks.

chunks.title: Glossary: Indian garments such as kurti, anarkali, lehenga and salwar suit
chunks.text: Bespoke knows these Indian garments, with the Hindi term printed on the Hindi tailor sheet. Kurti (कुर्ती) is a tunic top, and kurta is its longer or menswear form. Anarkali (अनारकली) is a long flared dress with a fitted top. Salwar suit (सलवार सूट) is a tunic with loose trousers and often a dupatta. Lehenga (लहंगा) is a long flared skirt, also called ghagra or chaniya choli. Saree blouse (ब्लाउज) is the fitted top worn with a saree, also called choli. Sherwani (शेरवानी) is a long formal coat. Nehru jacket (नेहरू जैकेट) is a short waistcoat or bandhgala.

chunks.title: Glossary: bottoms and drapes
chunks.text: Churidar (चूड़ीदार) is a fitted trouser that gathers at the ankle. Sharara (शरारा) is a wide, flared trouser with fullness from the knee. Palazzo (प्लाज़ो) is a wide straight trouser. Dhoti pants are draped trousers. Saree (साड़ी) is a long draped cloth and dupatta (दुपट्टा) is a long scarf worn with a suit or lehenga. Kurta set (कुर्ता सेट) is a kurta with matching bottoms. Skirt is स्कर्ट, trousers are पैंट, jeans are जींस, and leggings, joggers, shorts and cargo pants are also known.

chunks.title: Glossary: Western garments
chunks.text: Bespoke also knows everyday Western and winter wear: dress (ड्रेस), gown (गाउन), top (टॉप), shirt (शर्ट), t-shirt (टी-शर्ट), polo, tank top, crop top, corset, bodysuit, sweatshirt (स्वेटशर्ट), hoodie (हुडी), sweater (स्वेटर), cardigan (कार्डिगन), jacket (जैकेट), blazer (ब्लेज़र), coat (कोट), puffer jacket, shrug, cape, kaftan (कफ़्तान), jumpsuit (जंपसूट), co-ord set (को-ऑर्ड सेट), tracksuit, pyjama set and dungarees (डंगरी). In total there are 47 garment types.

chunks.title: Glossary: cotton and everyday fabrics
chunks.text: Cotton (सूती) is breathable and good for summer and daily wear. Mulmul (मलमल), also called muslin or malmal, is a very soft, light cotton. Linen (लिनन) is cool and crisp and creases easily. Khadi (खादी) is hand-spun, hand-woven cotton. Rayon (रेयॉन), which includes viscose and modal, drapes softly. Denim (डेनिम) is a sturdy cotton twill. Polyester (पॉलिएस्टर) and lycra (लाइक्रा) are used for stretch and sportswear. Bespoke lists cotton, linen, mulmul, rayon and chiffon as summer fabrics, and polyester, rayon, crepe and denim for the monsoon.

chunks.title: Glossary: silk, sheer and festive fabrics
chunks.text: Silk (रेशम), also called resham, is smooth and glossy. Banarasi (बनारसी), including brocade and jacquard, is a rich woven silk with patterns. Chanderi (चंदेरी) is a light sheer silk-cotton. Georgette (जॉर्जेट) and chiffon (शिफॉन) are light, flowing and slightly sheer. Organza (ऑर्गेंज़ा) is crisp and sheer. Crepe (क्रेप) has a fine crinkled texture. Satin (साटन) is glossy. Velvet (मखमल, also makhmal) is plush. Net (नेट) is an open mesh. These are common for weddings and festive wear.

chunks.title: Glossary: winter fabrics
chunks.text: For cold days Bespoke lists fleece (फ़्लीस), wool (ऊन), terry (टेरी), corduroy (कॉरडरॉय), velvet and flannel (फ़लालैन). Cashmere (कश्मीरी) is a very soft fine wool, and tweed (ट्वीड) is a rough woven wool. Leather (चमड़ा) and faux fur (फ़र) are also in the list. Terry, cotton, rayon and flannel suit loungewear, and lycra, polyester and cotton suit gym wear. If you say "for winter" or "for the cold", Bespoke treats it as the occasion and suggests fabrics for it.

chunks.title: Glossary: prints and embellishments
chunks.text: Prints include floral (फूलदार), striped (धारीदार), checked, polka dots, paisley (कैरी), bandhani (बांधनी, also bandhej or tie-dye), leheriya (लहरिया), block print, ikat (इकत), geometric and ombre. Embellishments include embroidery (कढ़ाई, also kadhai), zari (ज़री), gota patti (गोटा पत्ती), mirror work (शीशा काम), chikankari (चिकनकारी), sequins (सितारे), pearl work (मोती काम), zardozi (ज़रदोज़ी, also aari), thread work (धागा काम), lace (लेस), tassels (लटकन, latkan) and beadwork (मनके).

chunks.title: Glossary: body and part words in Hinglish
chunks.text: These Hindi words come up in everyday talk about clothes, and the first group is understood in your messages to Bespoke. Gala means neckline, peeth or peeche means back, baazu or aasteen means sleeve, kamar means waist, kulha means hip, kandha means shoulder, chaati means chest or bust, daman or ghera means hem or flare, and chaak means slit. Naap means measurement, darzi means tailor, kapda means cloth or fabric, and rang means colour. Direction words are neeche (below), upar (above), aage (front) and peeche (behind).

chunks.title: What Bespoke does not do
chunks.text: Bespoke does not sell clothes. It does not stock garments, take orders for ready-made products or run a shop. It helps you describe a garment clearly so that a tailor or maker can create it. If you want to compare with ready-made options, the app offers plain search links to shopping sites, but buying happens on those sites and not in Bespoke.

chunks.title: Prices and delivery
chunks.text: Bespoke does not give prices, quotes or delivery times. The cost of a garment and the time it takes depend on the maker, the fabric and the work involved, so ask the maker in the request chat. This assistant also does not know prices, so it cannot estimate them. If you ask about cost, the right step is to send the design to a maker and discuss it with them.

chunks.title: Pictures are suggestions
chunks.text: A picture on the moodboard is a suggestion, not an instruction. Bespoke reads only garment type, colour and print from a whole picture, and sleeve and neckline from a circled part. A photograph cannot show your fit, your measurements or the exact fabric, so those still come from you. If a picture suggests something you do not want, say so in words or edit the order card and your choice replaces it.

chunks.title: Where Bespoke can be wrong
chunks.text: Bespoke is built to be careful, but it can misread a message, especially an unusual phrase or heavy slang. It shows the words it understood and the value it chose for each part, so you can check and correct anything with a tap. The ease values on the tailor sheet are default starting values, not a promise about how the garment will fit, and your tailor may adjust them. Always confirm measurements and details with your tailor at the trial.

chunks.title: What this assistant can help with
chunks.text: This assistant helps with Bespoke only: describing a garment, using the moodboard, taking measurements, reading the tailor sheet, understanding ease and neckline depth, and working with a maker. It does not give medical, legal or financial advice, and it does not handle programming, general knowledge or news. If a question is outside Bespoke, it says so politely. If the help notes do not contain the answer, it tells you it does not know.

chunks.title: Where to get more help
chunks.text: If the assistant cannot answer, the most reliable next step for design questions is the main conversation, where Bespoke asks about each missing detail. For questions about a particular garment, such as a fabric or a stitching choice, ask the maker in the request chat or ask your tailor directly, because they know the practical limits of the work. Measurements are another good example: the guide in this assistant follows standard tailoring practice, but your tailor's own method comes first. Bespoke itself only produces the specification and the tailor sheet.

chunks.title: Sending a design to a maker
chunks.text: When your design is ready, you can send it to a maker, meaning a designer or tailor who has a Bespoke maker account. The maker receives your tailor sheet and your measurements as a request in their inbox. The pictures on your moodboard stay on your device and are not sent. Sending a design is how you ask a maker to look at it and, if they agree, to make it. Sending a design does not buy anything and does not fix a price; the maker decides whether to take it on and discusses the details with you in the chat.

chunks.title: What happens after you send your design
chunks.text: After you send a design it becomes a request with a status that you can follow. The maker reads it first. They may accept it, ask you for missing details, or decline it. If they need more information they flag what is missing and the request moves to Waiting on details. You answer in the chat, and the maker continues. Once accepted, the request moves on to Being made and then to Ready. You are able to talk to the maker in the chat at every stage.

chunks.title: Request statuses
chunks.text: A request is always in one of six statuses. New means you have sent it and the maker has not acted on it yet. Waiting on details means the maker has flagged something missing and is waiting for you. Accepted means the maker has agreed to make it. Being made means work has started. Ready means the garment is finished. Declined means the maker will not take the request, and you are free to send your design to another maker.

chunks.title: What Waiting on details means
chunks.text: Waiting on details means the maker needs something from you before they can go on. It usually means a measurement, a fabric, a colour or a length is missing, or a detail on the sheet is unclear. The maker flags exactly what is missing, so you know what to answer. Reply in the chat with the missing detail, or update your design and send it again. The request continues as soon as the maker has what they need.

chunks.title: How a maker flags missing details
chunks.text: A maker reading your request can flag the specific details that are missing, such as sleeve length, neckline depth, a body measurement or fabric. The flag is shown to you with the request, and the status changes to Waiting on details. This replaces the long call that a tailor would otherwise make to collect the same information. If you see a flag, look at the row it points to on the order card and fill it in.

chunks.title: Chatting with a maker
chunks.text: Each request has a chat between you and the maker. Use it to answer a flagged question, share a clarification, or talk through a detail such as a fabric choice. You can write in English or Hinglish, just like in the main conversation. The chat belongs to that request, so everything about one garment stays together in one place. Keep the chat polite and about the garment, and keep sensitive things like banking details out of it.

chunks.title: If a request is declined
chunks.text: A declined request means the maker will not take it on. Their reasons are the maker's own and may be about time, skills or the kind of garment. Declined does not mean the design is wrong. Your design and tailor sheet are still yours, and you can send the same design to a different maker or print the sheet and take it to a tailor of your choice.

chunks.title: Maker accounts
chunks.text: Makers have a separate account from customers. A maker signs in on their own and sees an inbox of requests sent to them, with the tailor sheet and measurements for each. From the inbox, the maker can accept or decline a request, flag missing details and chat with the customer. A customer account does not give access to the maker inbox. If you are a tailor or designer and want to receive requests, use the maker sign-in instead of the customer one.

chunks.title: The maker inbox
chunks.text: The maker inbox lists the requests that customers have sent to that maker, each with its status: New, Waiting on details, Accepted, Being made, Ready or Declined. Opening a request shows the tailor sheet part by part, next to the conversation with the customer. From there the maker can accept or decline the request, start making, mark the garment ready, or ask the customer for a detail that is missing.

chunks.title: Moving a request forward
chunks.text: The maker moves a request through its statuses as they work: they accept it, update it to Being made when work begins, and mark it Ready when the garment is finished. The customer sees the current status of the request. If something changes, for example a missing detail turns up, the maker can flag it, and the customer is told through the request and the chat.

chunks.title: How to measure: before you start
chunks.text: Use a soft tailor's tape and wear thin, close-fitting clothes or measure over underwear. Stand straight and relaxed, feet together, and breathe normally. Keep the tape snug and flat but not tight, with one finger's room underneath. Ask a friend to help if you can, because it is hard to read your own tape accurately. Write each measurement down in inches or centimetres, and say which one you used. Measure your body, not a garment: Bespoke adds the ease for the fit you choose.

chunks.title: How to measure your bust
chunks.text: Stand straight with your arms relaxed at your sides. Wrap the tape around the fullest part of your chest, across the bust points, and keep it level all the way around the back. It should sit flat and snug, not tight. Breathe normally and read the number where the tape meets the end. Wear the type of bra you plan to wear with the garment, because it changes the measurement. This is your bust or chest measurement, called chaati in Hindi.

chunks.title: How to measure your waist
chunks.text: Find your natural waist, which is the narrowest part of your torso, usually just above the belly button and below the ribs. Bend sideways and the crease that forms is a good guide. Wrap the tape around it, keep it level and snug, and breathe out normally without holding your stomach in. This is your waist measurement, called kamar in Hindi. If you want a skirt or trouser to sit lower, such as on the hip, measure there as well and tell the tailor.

chunks.title: How to measure your hip
chunks.text: Stand with your feet together and wrap the tape around the fullest part of your hips and seat, usually about eight inches below the natural waist. Keep the tape level all the way around, parallel to the floor, and snug but not tight. Check in a mirror that it does not dip at the back. This is your hip measurement, called kulha in Hindi. It matters most for fitted skirts, trousers, churidars and anything that is close at the hip.

chunks.title: How to measure your shoulder
chunks.text: The shoulder measurement runs across your back from the edge of one shoulder to the edge of the other, where the shoulder bone ends and the arm begins. Stand straight, find the bony point at the end of each shoulder, and measure along the back in a straight line over the top of the spine. Do not follow the curve of the back by pulling the tape tight. This is your shoulder, or kandha. It sets how the sleeve seam sits, so ask a helper to measure it.

chunks.title: How to measure sleeve length
chunks.text: Bend your arm slightly and measure from the edge of the shoulder, where the sleeve seam will sit, down the outside of your arm to where you want the sleeve to end: the elbow for elbow length, midway between the elbow and the wrist for three-quarter, or the wrist bone for full sleeves. For a short sleeve, measure to the point you like on the upper arm. Keep the tape loose enough that the arm can move freely.

chunks.title: How to measure garment length
chunks.text: For a kurti, dress or top, measure from the highest point of your shoulder, next to the neck, straight down the front over the bust to where you want the hem to end. Stand straight and keep the tape vertical. Use a mirror or a garment you already like as a guide: measure the same garment from the shoulder seam to the hem. Common endpoints are the hip, the knee, the calf, the ankle or the floor. Tell the tailor which one you mean.

chunks.title: Measuring a garment you already own
chunks.text: If a garment fits you well, lay it flat and measure it, then give those numbers to the tailor as a guide. Measure across the chest at the underarm, across the waist at its narrowest, across the hip at the fullest part, the shoulder seam to seam, the sleeve from shoulder seam to cuff, and the length from the top of the shoulder to the hem. Double the flat chest, waist and hip measurements to get the full circumference. This tells the tailor how much room you like, which is what ease means.

chunks.title: Measurement tips
chunks.text: Measure twice and use the same tape and units each time. Do not pull the tape tight and do not leave it loose. Measure in the same type of clothes and underwear that you will wear with the garment. Measure again if your size changes or the garment is for a different season, and ask your tailor to check at the trial. A tailor's own method may differ slightly from the ones described here, so follow their advice if they give you a different instruction.

chunks.title: What the moodboard is
chunks.text: The moodboard is a canvas where you pin pictures that show what you have in mind: a dress you saw, a sleeve you like, a colour. Bespoke reads the board together with your words and adds what it finds to the design. Pictures are suggestions. If a picture and your words disagree, your words win, and anything you edit or answer directly wins over both.

chunks.title: Pinning pictures
chunks.text: Add a picture to the board and Bespoke numbers the pictures in reading order, left to right and top to bottom, so you can refer to them as picture 1, #2 and so on. Pin as many as you need. A whole picture gives Bespoke the garment type, the colour and the print, and only when one reading is clearly better than the others. If a picture is unclear or shows several things, Bespoke leaves those rows alone rather than guess.

chunks.title: Circling a detail
chunks.text: To point at one part of a picture, draw a circle around it. A circled part tells Bespoke about the sleeve or the neckline in that picture. Bespoke looks at the circled area only, which is why a circle is more reliable than the whole picture for these two parts. A good habit is to circle the neckline you like on one picture and the sleeve you like on another, even if the garments differ.

chunks.title: Notes with arrows
chunks.text: Write a short note on the board and connect it to a picture with an arrow, or place it right next to the picture. Bespoke attaches the note to the picture it points at. For example, a note saying "this neckline" with an arrow to a circled neckline tells Bespoke which part you want to copy. Notes can be in English or Hinglish, just like the main conversation.

chunks.title: Saying "not this colour"
chunks.text: A negative note works as well as a positive one. If you like a dress but not its colour, write "not this colour" and attach it to the picture with an arrow. Bespoke then uses the garment and shape from the picture but will not take its colour, and it asks you for the colour you want instead. You can do the same with a print, a sleeve or a neckline by saying "not this sleeve" or "not this print".

chunks.title: Comparing pictures: "deeper than #1"
chunks.text: You can compare pictures instead of giving numbers. A note such as "neckline deeper than #1" or "deeper than #1 but less than #2" is turned into a range in inches using the neckline depths of those pictures. Bespoke proposes a value toward the shallow end of the range, because a neckline can be deepened at the trial but never raised. If the pictures contradict each other, for example if #2 is shallower than #1 but you want the neckline between them, Bespoke asks you instead of guessing.

chunks.title: What a whole picture gives and what a circle gives
chunks.text: A whole picture gives garment type, colour and print. A circled part gives sleeve and neckline. Other details, such as fit, length and fabric, are not read from pictures, because a photograph cannot show them reliably; Bespoke asks you for those or uses your words. This keeps the specification honest: only what a picture can really show is taken from it.

chunks.title: Pictures suggest, words win
chunks.text: Everything read from a picture is marked on the order card as a suggestion from the board. If you later say something different in words, such as "make it green", the green replaces what the picture suggested. If you tap a row on the order card and pick a value, that choice replaces both. The order in which Bespoke trusts things is: your edit on the order card, your answer to a question, your words, a note on the board, a picture, and finally any stored profile.

chunks.title: Privacy: where your words and pictures are read
chunks.text: Bespoke reads your words and your moodboard pictures in your own browser. A trained language model that tags garment words and a picture model both run on your device, so understanding what you wrote and what a picture shows does not depend on sending them anywhere. It works instantly and keeps working without a network connection once the page has loaded.

chunks.title: The optional language model
chunks.text: Bespoke can optionally ask an outside language model to help with a request that its own on-device reading cannot name, such as an unusual phrase. When that is switched on, the text of your message and a short summary of the current design go to the model through a server function. If it is not configured, slow or failing, Bespoke carries on with its own on-device answer and you see no error. Whatever the model returns is checked against Bespoke's own list of garment words before it is used.

chunks.title: What this help assistant does with your question
chunks.text: This help assistant works the same way: your question is checked for safety, personal details such as email addresses, mobile numbers and long digit strings are masked, and the question is matched against Bespoke's help notes. Only when the notes cover your question is a language model asked to phrase the answer. Please do not type personal details, passwords or payment information into the assistant, because it never needs them.

chunks.title: Customer and maker accounts
chunks.text: Customers and makers use separate sign-ins. A maker only sees the requests that customers have sent to that maker. When you send a design, you share the specification and chat with that maker. If you do not want to share a design, do not send it; you can still use the tailor sheet on your own and print it for any tailor you choose.

chunks.title: Where your designs and boards are kept
chunks.text:
When you are logged in, your designs and moodboards are saved to your Bespoke account, so they open again on any device. Moodboard pictures are kept in private storage that only your account can read, and nobody else, makers included, can see your designs or boards unless you send a design to a maker.

When you are not logged in, your design lasts only while the browser tab is open, and a new tab starts a fresh design. Moodboards are kept in this browser on this device. The next time you log in on that device, those boards move to your account. Nothing you make while logged out is sent to Bespoke's servers.

chunks.title: The tailor sheet
chunks.text: The tailor sheet is a printable page that lists every instruction for the garment, part by part: garment, neckline shape and depth, sleeves, fit, length, fabric, colour, details and any notes. Each line shows where it came from, so a tailor can tell your own words from a default. It prints to A4 or saves as a PDF. Drawings of the chosen neckline, sleeves, shape and length are shown beside the instructions where drawings are available. The sheet appears in the conversation once the design is complete.

chunks.title: English and Hindi sheets
chunks.text: You can switch the tailor sheet between English and Hindi. The switch is complete: part names, values, labels and the finished measurements all change language, for example neckline becomes गले का आकार and sleeve length becomes आस्तीन की लंबाई. This helps when your tailor reads Hindi more comfortably than English. You can print either version, and you can print both to keep one for yourself.

chunks.title: Finished measurement equals body plus ease
chunks.text: The sheet shows finished measurements, which are the size of the garment once it is sewn, not the size of your body. A finished measurement is your body measurement plus ease, the extra room a fit needs. A fitted bodice has less ease and a loose one has more. Bespoke adds the ease for the fit you chose to the body measurements you entered, so the tailor can cut directly from the sheet without doing the sum.

chunks.title: Ease: what it means
chunks.text: Ease is the extra room between your body and the garment. Without ease, a garment would be exactly as big as your body and you could not breathe, sit or lift your arms comfortably. Ease depends on the fit you ask for. The more relaxed the fit, the more ease the tailor adds to your measurement. Ease is added to the bust, waist and hip according to the fit chosen for the upper and lower parts of the garment.

chunks.title: Ease numbers Bespoke uses
chunks.text: Bespoke uses these default ease allowances, in inches: fitted 1.5, semi-fitted 2.5, relaxed 3.5 and loose 5. For example, a fitted kurti with a 34 inch bust comes out at 35.5 inches finished, and a loose one at 39 inches. These are starting values shown as defaults on the sheet, to be replaced by partner tailors' own values over time. If your tailor works differently, tell them; the sheet marks the ease as a default so that they know it is adjustable.

chunks.title: Fit words and what they mean
chunks.text: Bespoke uses four fits. Fitted is close to the body, with the least ease, similar to words like snug, tight or body hugging. Semi-fitted is slightly eased, like a regular fit. Relaxed is comfortable and easy, and not tight. Loose is roomy, including words like dheela, baggy, flowy, oversized or boxy. You can give a fit for the upper body and a different one for the lower part, such as fitted at the waist and loose below, and you can soften it with "thoda".

chunks.title: Neckline depth: what it means
chunks.text: Neckline depth is how far down the front neckline drops. Bespoke uses four depths in inches: shallow 4.5, moderate 6, deep 7.5 and plunging 9. A word like "thoda deep" falls between moderate and deep, which is about 6.75 inches. Neckline depth is one of the most important details to get right, because a neckline that is cut too deep cannot be raised again, while one that is too shallow can be deepened at the trial. This is why Bespoke asks about it early and proposes the shallower value when it is unsure.

chunks.title: Neckline shapes
chunks.text: Besides depth, a neckline has a shape. Bespoke knows round (gol gala), V, deep V, boat, square (chaukor), sweetheart, halter, high neck, mandarin collar, keyhole, off-shoulder, U, collar, cowl, potli, crew, hooded and turtle necks. Pick the shape first and the depth second. A round neck and a deep V can both be described as deep, but they look very different. If you are not sure, circle a neckline on a picture in the moodboard and Bespoke will suggest the nearest one.

chunks.title: Sleeve length and style
chunks.text: Sleeve length is separate from sleeve style. Bespoke has six lengths: sleeveless, cap, short, elbow, three-quarter and full. Styles include puff, bell, bishop (also called balloon), flutter, cold shoulder, kimono (also batwing or dolman), raglan, straight and sheer. Sleeve length is asked about because a sleeve cut too short cannot be lengthened. You can say, for example, "three-quarter sleeves, bell style" or "baazu chhote".

chunks.title: Garment length
chunks.text: Garment length is how far down the garment reaches. Bespoke uses seven steps from shortest to longest: crop, hip, short, knee, midi, ankle and floor. In Hinglish, "ghutne tak" means to the knee, "lamba" or "lambi" means long and "chhota" means short. Length is asked about because fabric that is cut short cannot be made longer. If you are unsure, tell the tailor the point on your body where you want the hem to end, and use a picture as a guide.

chunks.title: What the sheet does not contain
chunks.text: The tailor sheet is a specification, not a price quote or an order confirmation. It does not include a price, a delivery date or a guarantee about the result. Finished measurements depend on the body measurements you give. Bring the sheet to your tailor and let them confirm the details at the trial. If something on the sheet looks wrong, go back to the order card, tap the row, pick the right value and open the sheet again; the sheet always reflects the current design, so there is nothing to fix on the printed page itself.
